objective.statement: Name the primary chords in a short passage, in a major or minor key.
successCriteria: I find the key, then the lowest note of each marked chord.
I say which degree that note is and so which chord it is.
I use the harmonic minor in a minor key.

explanation.text: In an examination you are not asked to write chords in a passage; you may be asked to name some. The chords are always tonic, subdominant or dominant, always in root position. All you need to know is the key, and which degree of its scale the bottom note of each chord is.

music.textAlternative: Three bars in G major: a chord of G, B and D; a chord of C, E and G; a chord of D, F sharp and A.

explanation.caption: G major: G is the 1st degree (I), C the 4th (IV), D the 5th (V).

explanation.text: Method: (1) find the key from the key signature. (2) For each marked chord, find the lowest note. (3) Count to see which degree of the scale it is: 1 is the tonic, 4 the subdominant and 5 the dominant. In a minor key remember the harmonic minor: a chord on the 5th degree is a dominant even if it has the raised leading note.

Spacing and doubling can make a chord look different, but the lowest note still gives the answer. Take care in minor keys: the dominant chord has an accidental, the raised 7th, which is not in the key signature.
Key, lowest note, degree: 1 = tonic, 4 = subdominant, 5 = dominant.

music.textAlternative: Two bars of A minor: the dominant, E, G sharp, B; then the tonic, A, C, E.

steps: The key signature has no sharps or flats: A minor, the relative of C major.
The first chord has E at the bottom, the 5th degree: the dominant.
The second has A at the bottom, the tonic.
demonstration.textAlternative: The dominant and tonic chords of A minor.

guided.prompt: This passage is in D♭ major. Every chord is in root position. Which marked chord in the passage is the dominant chord (V)?

music.textAlternative: Treble stave. Bar 1 (chord A): in the 3rd space. Bar 2 (chord B): on the 4th line with a flat sign; on the 1st ledger line above the stave with a flat sign. Bar 3 (chord C): a rest. Bar 4 (chord D): a rest.

Bass stave. Bar 1: in the 1st space with a flat sign; on the 5th line with a flat sign; on the 2nd ledger line above the stave with a flat sign. Bar 2: on the 3rd line with a flat sign; in the space above the 2nd ledger line above the stave. Bar 3: on the 1st line with a flat sign; in the space just above the stave with a flat sign; in the space above the 1st ledger line above the stave with a flat sign. Bar 4: in the space below the 1st ledger line below the stave with a flat sign; on the 5th line with a flat sign; in the space above the 2nd ledger line above the stave.

B.reason: Chord B is the tonic chord (I): its root is degree 1 of the scale. The dominant chord is built on degree 5.

C.reason: Chord C is the subdominant chord (IV): its root is degree 4 of the scale. The dominant chord is built on degree 5.

D.reason: Chord D is the tonic chord (I): its root is degree 1 of the scale. The dominant chord is built on degree 5.

hints: Find the root of each chord.
Find the root (the lowest note) of each chord and say which degree of D♭ major it is. The dominant is degree 5.

feedback.correct: Yes: you found each root first.

mistakes.wrong-degree: Chord I is on degree 1, IV on 4 and V on 5.
mistakes.root-confused-with-bass: The lowest note isn't always the root. Stack the notes in 3rds to find it, then check the inversion.
mistakes.inversion-misread: Inversion depends on which note of the triad is in the bass: root (a), 3rd (b) or 5th (c).
mistakes.leading-note-not-raised: In minor keys, chords use the harmonic minor, so the leading note is raised.
mistakes.note-missing: One of the notes doesn't belong. A triad has a root, a 3rd and a 5th.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Find the root first, then the bass note.
